tabs.title: Part Overview
tabs.text:
TECH UNIT 5 — PART 2 OF 3: STORY & ART — canonical DayID family 30503
This is NOT a new game. Students open the SAME playable geometry-only TurboWarp prototype from 30502, invent a meaningful original world, and replace the shape costumes/backdrop without rewriting or breaking the shared working mechanics. The purpose is design, storytelling, art and audience communication, not advanced independent code.
TEKS: Primary §126.18(c)(3)(B–C) planning/testing/industry and (4)(C) transfer; supporting (1)(C,E) abstraction and testing. Student choices must remain meaningful but accessible; do not infer TurboWarp alone satisfies text-based nested-loop §126.18(c)(2)(B).
Day1 STARTER 3050301: story map with protagonist, setting, conflict, objective; DAILY key 305030130064.
Day2 PERFORM 3050302: original player/falling object costumes, silhouette and contrast; DAILY key 305030230065.
Day3 PERFORM 3050303: replace visuals, stage background, title/instructions and test original loop/collisions; DAILY key 305030330066.
Day4 ASSESSMENT 3050304: compact four-section MAJOR keys 305030439991–305030439994 followed by time for earlier Daily recovery.
Day5 MILESTONE/RECOVERY 3050305: complete and submit SAME game with original story/visuals, recover posted weak Major/Daily sections. NO new mastery.
One Major = equal-weight mean of 4 graded section responses using existing Collector Assessment Sections and Skyward MAJOR. DAILY keys in Collector Question Bank must match exact source questions/rubrics. 50-minute days; short novice writing, substantial creative work, accessibility and copyright protections. Story does NOT require a new programming mechanism until Part 3.
Release gates: Part outline→local Collector pin→canonical master HTML→curriculum/code/functional/offline/visual QA→same-byte JISD copy→Captain release. Student visibility unchanged. SOURCE OUTLINE ONLY; HTML NOT DONE.
Mode reconciliation — approved source repair 2026-11-12: Preserve the Captain-approved same-game daily tasks and dominant mode. Prototype Day 2's player controls are isolated teacher-guided new-tool practice within LEARN, not an additional independent project. On PERFORM days, place brief retrieval and the exact supported recipe in the work runway; do not add a second general Group Learn workload. Source teaching and tested code instructions remain available beside the required work. The approved Part-specific progression governs this build; no DayID, pinned question/rubric or milestone is changed.

tabs.title: Day 1
tabs.text:
DAY 1 | DAYID 3050301 | STARTER | Give the Game a World
LEARNING TARGET: I can develop a character, world and meaningful game goal because a playable rule can communicate a story.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
TIME: 4 min independent Warm-Up; 12 min Group Learn with teacher visual example; 6 min Group Practice; 7 min DAILY question; 16 min story/art Perform; 5 min save/check and one Creative Studio choice. Adapt if real editing takes longer; preserve actual student production.
WARM-UP (Xtra key 305030109998): Imagine a circle falling from the sky. Is it a treasure, hazard, message or something else? Who cares about it?
LEARN: You already have a playable Falling Objects prototype. The SQUARE is your unnamed main character, the CIRCLE is an event or object, and the empty stage is an unbuilt world. A GAME PITCH is a short explanation of WHO, WHERE, WHY and WHAT CHANGES. Storyboarding ties the existing mechanic to a motivation: catching supplies, dodging meteors, rescuing animals or collecting ideas all use identical game code but suggest different emotional stakes. Make one hero, one world, one challenge and one player goal. Story can be funny, beautiful, mysterious or realistic; it must be original, school-appropriate and legible for a chosen audience. Art replaces geometry LATER, not today.
GROUP PRACTICE: Compare a plain square dodging a circle against a librarian saving books from a leaky ceiling. The basic mechanic remains identical; class identifies how the goal, setting, stakes and naming changed the meaning without adding code.
DAILY ACADEMIC QUESTION — FULL KEY 305030130064: A game has a moving square, falling circles, a score and three lives. Invent a main character, setting and conflict that give those SAME mechanics meaning. Explain what the circles represent and why the player cares.
PINNED RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 clear, original, specific and strongly justified design reasoning; 70–89 Includes coherent character, place, motivation and meaningful interpretation of existing falling rules; 50–69 incomplete or weakly explained; below 50 not enough relevant evidence. Missing/unsubmitted is tracked separately rather than invented as automatic numerical zero.
INDEPENDENT QUESTION VALIDITY: Askable from taught examples without needing student's project to be finished. At most ONE brief typed response. The capture-first engine records every field even when incomplete; no academic completeness submission gate.
PERFORM (single continuing game): In a paper or teacher-approved editor create a one-page Story Map: game title, target audience, protagonist, two-sentence backstory, conflict, circle meaning, player objective, mood/colors and 3 thumbnail scene ideas. Keep existing TurboWarp file saved and unchanged. Identify what square/circle/background will later become.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required separate Xtra response; student chooses from three): Brainstorm three different worlds using the same mechanic; write a villain monologue; draw a tiny concept thumbnail.
TEKS TEMPERATURE: confidence thumbs and optional specific gap; separate participation evidence, not TEKS score.
MILESTONE: Complete story map connects existing mechanics to original character/world and audience.
SUBMISSION: Original question through school Form; editable artifact through confirmed class assignment only. Never invent an assignment or claim an external art file was saved when unverified.

tabs.title: Day 2
tabs.text:
DAY 2 | DAYID 3050302 | PERFORM | Design Readable Character Art
LEARNING TARGET: I can draw distinctive sprites with simple digital tools because clear silhouettes and contrast help players understand a game quickly.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(C): Explain how an algorithm can be generalized to solve other problems.
TIME: 4 min independent Warm-Up; 12 min Group Learn with teacher visual example; 6 min Group Practice; 7 min DAILY question; 16 min story/art Perform; 5 min save/check and one Creative Studio choice. Adapt if real editing takes longer; preserve actual student production.
WARM-UP (Xtra key 305030209998): Which is easier to recognize while moving: a detailed tiny drawing or a bold silhouette? Explain one visual clue.
LEARN: A sprite COSTUME can change what an object looks like without rewriting its CODE. Demonstrate TurboWarp's Costumes tab: select Player, duplicate its original geometric costume as backup, choose drawing tools (rectangle, oval, line, fill, eraser), adjust fill/outline and draw an original hero. A strong silhouette is recognizable small, contrast separates it from the background, and costume dimensions/center matter for apparent collision. Select FallingObject separately and create its story-world object using the same tools. Use original school-appropriate art; do not fetch copyrighted characters or external assets. Clear design matters more than technical drawing talent.
GROUP PRACTICE: Teacher shows two silhouettes: a low-contrast flat hero and a high-contrast hero; class identifies which stands out. Students test a 40% zoom stage-view to see if sprite reads at game speed. Demonstrate saving a backup costume BEFORE editing.
DAILY ACADEMIC QUESTION — FULL KEY 305030230065: A student replaces a square player with a complicated dark character on a dark stage and can no longer find it during play. Recommend TWO specific visual changes that would improve recognition while preserving the game's story.
PINNED RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 clear, original, specific and strongly justified design reasoning; 70–89 Proposes two relevant, concrete silhouette/contrast/scale/hierarchy improvements tied to quick recognition; 50–69 incomplete or weakly explained; below 50 not enough relevant evidence. Missing/unsubmitted is tracked separately rather than invented as automatic numerical zero.
INDEPENDENT QUESTION VALIDITY: Askable from taught examples without needing student's project to be finished. At most ONE brief typed response. The capture-first engine records every field even when incomplete; no academic completeness submission gate.
PERFORM (single continuing game): From story map, design original Player and FallingObject costumes in TurboWarp, each with a saved basic-shape backup. Keep them recognizable while moving. Add a simple original or solid-color backdrop in Stage Backdrops, making sure art does not obscure score/lives. Leave motion, loops and scoring scripts UNCHANGED. Save SAME project.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required separate Xtra response; student chooses from three): Create an alternate expressive face costume; compare outline strengths; draw a tiny icon that would make lives more readable.
TEKS TEMPERATURE: confidence thumbs and optional specific gap; separate participation evidence, not TEKS score.
MILESTONE: Two original readable story-themed sprites are visible and scripts preserved.
SUBMISSION: Original question through school Form; editable artifact through confirmed class assignment only. Never invent an assignment or claim an external art file was saved when unverified.

tabs.title: Day 3
tabs.text:
DAY 3 | DAYID 3050303 | PERFORM | Replace Art Without Breaking Gameplay
LEARNING TARGET: I can test a game after changing its visuals because design refinements must preserve working interactions.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm.
TIME: 4 min independent Warm-Up; 12 min Group Learn with teacher visual example; 6 min Group Practice; 7 min DAILY question; 16 min story/art Perform; 5 min save/check and one Creative Studio choice. Adapt if real editing takes longer; preserve actual student production.
WARM-UP (Xtra key 305030309998): If a larger costume is drawn around a sprite, which game rule might change accidentally?
LEARN: Replacing artwork can affect the player's perception, sprite centers, visible size and TOUCHING checks even when code has not changed. Review the original prototype's five functional tests: restart position, left/right control, repeated drop, exactly one life lost per hit, score once per safe dodge. Use a BACKUP costume rather than deleting geometry; test at consistent stage scale. Show UI labels for controls, lives and score; add a simple readable title or story sentence on stage as appropriate. Visual clarity and fair gameplay are both design responsibilities. Distinguish visual fixes (contrast, silhouette, background) from mechanic changes (collision rules), which come in Part 3.
GROUP PRACTICE: Teacher intentionally enlarges an obstacle costume, demonstrates apparent hit-box change, restores suitable costume center/size and reruns one collision. Class records expected/actual result and whether the change was visual or logical.
DAILY ACADEMIC QUESTION — FULL KEY 305030330066: After a student replaces a small circle with a large spaceship costume, the player loses lives from what looks like a distant hit. Name TWO checks or changes that could correct this and describe how you would retest it without rewriting the entire game.
PINNED RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 clear, original, specific and strongly justified design reasoning; 70–89 Correctly identifies plausible collision/size/center/costume issue and describes a repeatable test with original mechanics; 50–69 incomplete or weakly explained; below 50 not enough relevant evidence. Missing/unsubmitted is tracked separately rather than invented as automatic numerical zero.
INDEPENDENT QUESTION VALIDITY: Askable from taught examples without needing student's project to be finished. At most ONE brief typed response. The capture-first engine records every field even when incomplete; no academic completeness submission gate.
PERFORM (single continuing game): Replace all shape placeholders with original character and falling-object costumes, add themed background and a readable 1–2-sentence world/goal introduction. Rerun every five-item prototype test and record one observed art-related issue plus fix. Retain same project and preserve working code. Save milestone version after tests.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required separate Xtra response; student chooses from three): Design a story-setting sign; experiment with two backdrop colors; write a dramatic one-line title screen description.
TEKS TEMPERATURE: confidence thumbs and optional specific gap; separate participation evidence, not TEKS score.
MILESTONE: Playable same game now tells an original story with readable art and preserved mechanics.
SUBMISSION: Original question through school Form; editable artifact through confirmed class assignment only. Never invent an assignment or claim an external art file was saved when unverified.

tabs.title: Day 4
tabs.text:
DAY 4 | DAYID 3050304 | ASSESSMENT / EARLIER DAILY RECOVERY | Storytelling & Visual Design
LEARNING TARGET: I can explain how story, audience, visual hierarchy and evidence-driven revision help a functional game communicate meaning.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm.
GRADE: one MAJOR = equally weighted four short holistic sections; keys 305030439991–305030439994. Each section separately copied and submitted via established school Form, with a real receipt. About 25 minutes for review, reading, answering and four Form trips; remaining time for previous Daily recovery. No new ordinary mastery QIDs or game building during test.
PARTIAL STUDY & RECALL (usable during test; no scenario answers): protagonist, setting, conflict, objective, audience, silhouette, contrast, visual hierarchy, sprite costume, stage backdrop, scale, code preservation, control test, targeted revision. Purposeful visual design makes game interactions intelligible.
SECTION 1: Story Connected to Mechanics
FULL KEY 305030439991
STUDENT PROMPT: The same game has a player and one falling hazard. (A) Write one original protagonist and setting. (B) Explain how the falling hazard creates a story conflict without changing the basic code.
PINNED HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 coherent original protagonist, setting, stakes and causal link to mechanics; 70–89 clear character/world and logical mechanic-conflict connection; 50–69 missing one essential connection; below 50 insufficient.
One concise accessible response; explicitly copy empty/partial parts rather than block submission. No project work in assessed section.

SECTION 2: Audience and Readable Design
FULL KEY 305030439992
STUDENT PROMPT: A younger player cannot distinguish the hero from the background. (A) Choose a silhouette or color-contrast change. (B) Explain why that change helps that audience during quick gameplay.
PINNED HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 specific audience-centered contrast/silhouette reasoning and feasible design choice; 70–89 relevant visual change and clear player benefit; 50–69 vague or weakly connected; below 50 insufficient.
One concise accessible response; explicitly copy empty/partial parts rather than block submission. No project work in assessed section.

SECTION 3: Changing Costumes Safely
FULL KEY 305030439993
STUDENT PROMPT: A new costume looks larger and the collision seems unfair. (A) Name one way to check sprite size, center or costume placement. (B) Say what gameplay test you would repeat after fixing it.
PINNED HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 precise visual/technical diagnostic and controlled test tied to collision behavior; 70–89 plausible check and relevant repeated test; 50–69 one correct element only; below 50 insufficient.
One concise accessible response; explicitly copy empty/partial parts rather than block submission. No project work in assessed section.

SECTION 4: Critique and Revision
FULL KEY 305030439994
STUDENT PROMPT: Two students play your new story game. One can understand the goal; the other says the falling objects blend in. (A) Identify the more actionable feedback. (B) Describe a targeted visual revision and one way to check whether it worked.
PINNED HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 evidence-based choice, targeted revision and sound verification; 70–89 recognizes a useful problem, change and test; 50–69 partly reasoned; below 50 insufficient.
One concise accessible response; explicitly copy empty/partial parts rather than block submission. No project work in assessed section.

TEKS TEMPERATURE: thumbs for story/goal, audience, shapes/contrast, costume changes, and testing; separately submitted under 305030429999.
CREATIVE STUDIO: one fun taught-tool choice—design an original title sticker, alternate villain silhouette, or game-goal icon—and describe it in separate Xtra under 305030420000. It does not increase the Major.
AFTER ASSESSMENT: Use posted grades for earlier DAILY questions on the ORIGINAL DayIDs; no newly given Major recovery until scored feedback is available. Before Day5 post the new Major grade/section feedback or reschedule its recovery.
QA: exact pinned assessments in Collector, real shared submission controls, source/offline parity, no release before Captain.

tabs.title: Day 5
tabs.text:
DAY 5 | DAYID 3050305 | STORY & ART MILESTONE + MAJOR/DAILY RECOVERY
LEARNING TARGET: I can finish an expressive, readable game world while keeping the underlying gameplay reliable because creative stories still need functioning technology.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm.
FIRST HALF (~25 min): Open SAME saved TurboWarp project, use Story Map as checklist. Complete original protagonist and falling-object costumes, audience-appropriate background, title and simple story-driven objective. Confirm no old placeholder-only visual remains visible except backup costumes, preserve uniform game code and verify five functions: movement, falls, one-life hit, one-score dodge and reset. Test with another student if classroom access allows, revise one art issue and save the SAME editable game. Submit only through the existing teacher-confirmed assignment (do not invent an URL).
SECOND HALF (~25 min): Read the posted Skyward Major score and section-specific comments. Recover only missing/weaker original 3050304 sections through Day4 original Form routes and any earlier weak DAILY questions through their original DayIDs. Stronger verified evidence updates the SAME grade/section, not an effort bonus. If posted Major feedback is delayed, move that recovery slot and continue authentic Daily recovery and constructive work instead.
MILESTONE CRITERIA: recognizably original title/world/hero/conflict, matched falling object, readable stage and HUD, working shared mechanics, documented test and one revision.
CREATIVE STUDIO: optional original story teaser, alternative costume, or level-sketch as separate Xtra only when adequate time; no new mastery key and no second Major.
NEXT PART: Maintain this very project for Phase 3 unique gameplay mechanic. Student visibility remains Captain-controlled.
